title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Ulnar neuropathy constitutes a common upper-extremity compression neuropathy with multiple potential entrapment sites along the nerve’s course. The elbow, particularly the cubital tunnel, accounts for most cases of ulnar neuropathy, although clinically significant compression may also occur at the wrist within the Guyon canal, as well as in the forearm or upper arm. This course outlines the etiologic factors of ulnar neuropathy, including prolonged elbow flexion, external pressure, anatomic variants, trauma, repetitive motion, and mass lesions, as well as the factors that can increase risk, such as occupational strain, metabolic disease, and previous upper-extremity injury. The pathophysiology of this condition, involving mechanical deformation, ischemia, and impaired axonal transport, producing demyelination or axonal loss, is also discussed.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Participants will gain an understanding of ulnar neuropathy's clinical manifestations, including paresthesias of the fourth and fifth digits, hand weakness, impaired grip and pinch strength, and, in advanced disease, intrinsic muscle atrophy, as well as the diagnostic processes that rely on a focused clinical evaluation supported by electrodiagnostic studies and imaging when structural causes are suspected, the management strategies, and the complications including persistent sensory loss, motor deficits, or progressive deformity. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying ulnar neuropathy, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition, ultimately improving clinical outcomes and reducing morbidity.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: The ulnar nerve has multiple potential compression sites along its course. Although the elbow is the most common site of compression, clinically significant injury may also occur at the wrist, forearm, and upper arm. Prevention of compression, along with early diagnosis and treatment, is essential for optimizing prognosis, as treatment outcomes are often disappointing once axonal damage has developed.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: The C8 and T1 nerve roots merge to form the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. This trunk continues as the medial cord and gives rise to the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve then courses along the upper arm medial to the brachial artery and in proximity to the median nerve. At the middle and lower 3rd of the arm, the ulnar nerve passes through the Arcade of Struthers, a fibrous canal composed of the medial head of the triceps brachii muscle and its aponeurotic expansion, which extends into the intermuscular septum and the internal brachial ligament. [1] [2]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: At the elbow, the ulnar nerve courses posteriorly and enters the retroepicondylar groove between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon process. The nerve then enters the cubital tunnel through the cubital tunnel retinaculum (CTR), a band approximately 4 mm wide attached from the medial epicondyle to the olecranon at the proximal edge of the tunnel roof. Distally, the nerve passes beneath the humeroulnar aponeurotic arcade, also known as the Osborne band, a dense aponeurosis between the tendon attachments of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU). [3] The area beneath the humeroulnar aponeurotic arcade constitutes the cubital tunnel (see Image . Osborne Ligament in the Cubital Tunnel). The nerve then traverses the belly of the FCU muscle and exits through the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: At the forearm, the ulnar nerve innervates the FCU and the flexor digitorum profundus. At the midforearm to distal forearm, the palmar ulnar cutaneous (PUC) branch separates and enters the hand ventral to the Guyon canal, providing sensory innervation to the hypothenar skin. Distal to the PUC bifurcation, the dorsal ulnar cutaneous (DUC) branch emerges from the main trunk, curves around the ulna, and supplies sensory innervation to the dorsal medial hand, the medial one-half of the fourth digit, and the fifth digit.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: The main trunk of the ulnar nerve enters the Guyon canal at the level of the distal wrist crease. The proximal wall of the canal is formed by the pisiform bone, and the distal wall by the hook of the hamate. The roof consists of the palmaris brevis muscle, while the floor is formed by the transverse carpal ligament, the hamate, and the triquetrum bone. At the canal outlet, the pisohamate hiatus forms a thick band connecting the hook of the hamate to the pisiform bone. Within the Guyon canal, the ulnar nerve separates into a superficial sensory branch and a deep palmar motor branch. The superficial sensory branch provides sensory innervation to the palmar aspects of the medial one-half of the fourth digit and the fifth digit.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Introduction
content: Before exiting through the pisohamate hiatus, motor fibers branch from the deep palmar motor branch to innervate the hypothenar muscles, including the abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, opponens digiti minimi, and palmaris brevis. The deep palmar branch further provides motor innervation to the adductor pollicis, deep head of the flexor pollicis brevis, third and fourth lumbricals, and the 3 palmar and 4 dorsal interossei. [4]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Etiology
content: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (UNE) represents the second most common upper-extremity entrapment neuropathy. Compression of the nerve beneath the cubital tunnel is termed "cubital tunnel syndrome" (CTS).

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Etiology
content: At the elbow, the ulnar nerve lacks protective coverage within the ulnar groove, rendering it vulnerable to external compression. Additional lesions that may compromise nerve integrity include anomalous muscles, chronic traction, scar tissue, and arthritic changes. An increased carrying angle constitutes a recognized risk factor for nontraumatic ulnar neuropathy. [5] In certain individuals, the ulnar nerve may sublux medially over the medial epicondyle during elbow flexion. Repetitive subluxation can produce friction neuritis, contributing to progressive neuropathic injury.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Etiology
content: As mentioned, the CTR is located at the proximal edge of the cubital tunnel. O'Driscoll classified the CTR into 4 types. Type 0 represents an absent retinaculum. Type Ia is characterized by a lax retinaculum in elbow extension that becomes taut in full flexion. Type Ib consists of a retinaculum that is tight in positions short of full flexion, typically 90° to 120°. Type II occurs when the anconeus epitrochlearis muscle replaces the retinaculum.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Etiology
content: O'Driscoll postulated that Type 0 permits ulnar displacement due to the absence of the retinaculum. Type Ia is considered normal and does not contribute to ulnar neuropathy. Type Ib predisposes the nerve to dynamic compression forces, whereas type II may produce static compression owing to muscle bulk. [6] Pressures measured between the ulnar nerve and the humeroulnar arcade increase to above 200 mm Hg during elbow flexion or isometric contraction of the FCU. In contrast, pressure remains below 19 mm Hg during elbow extension. [7]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Etiology
content: Repetitive movements exerting pressure on the ulnar wrist and hypothenar eminence increase susceptibility to cumulative stress ulnar neuropathy. Traumatic events, eg, distal radial or wrist fractures, and space-occupying lesions, including ganglion cysts, may also produce ulnar neuropathy at the wrist (UNW). [8]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Epidemiology
content: A study reported an incidence of CTS in the United States of 30 per 100,000 person-years. [9] In a metropolitan United States cohort, 5.9% of participants were identified with this condition. [10] Crude prevalence rates in Egypt demonstrated that UNE was the second most common entrapment neuropathy. [11] A nationwide registry study in Finland reported total crude incidence rates of 26 and 36 per 100,000 person-years among men and women, respectively. [12]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Epidemiology
content: Ulnar nerve injury may result from traction, compression, or trauma. However, the majority of ulnar neuropathies are nontraumatic, with approximately 50% of cases occurring on the left side, irrespective of handedness. [13] [14] Risk factors for UNE include male sex (odds ratio = 2.4), older age, smoking history, elevated body mass index, diabetes, polyneuropathies, and sustained pressure on a flexed elbow. [15] [16] [17] UNE risk increases in a dose-dependent manner with cigarette pack-years, with more than 10 pack-years increasing risk over 5-fold. [18]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Epidemiology
content: Repetitive elbow flexion and prolonged pressure predispose to ulnar neuropathy. Postoperative neuropathy may occur following anesthesia or surgery, underscoring the need for proper intraoperative positioning. [19] Certain sports and activities further increase susceptibility, including wheelchair marathon participation—particularly in individuals with ulnar nerve subluxation—cycling, and tennis. [20] [21] [22] [23]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Pathophysiology
content: Ulnar neuropathy arises from multiple etiologies. According to the Seddon classification of nerve injuries, neuropraxia represents the mildest form, characterized by focal segmental demyelination and a high likelihood of full recovery. Axonotmesis involves injury to the axon while preserving the connective tissue framework, resulting in a variable rate of recovery. Neurotmesis constitutes complete transection of the nerve and carries a poor prognosis, with functional recovery typically requiring surgical intervention.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- History and Physical
content: Symptoms of UNE typically develop gradually unless associated with trauma. Numbness and paresthesia may radiate distally to the ulnar aspect of the hand, the fifth digit, and the ulnar one-half of the fourth digit. Symptoms are often exacerbated by elbow flexion, particularly at night. Pain is generally not prominent unless an acute injury arises, although overuse of the forearm flexors, such as the FCU, may produce discomfort.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- History and Physical
content: Sensory involvement of the fifth digit and the medial one-half of the fourth digit may also indicate UNW. However, similar findings can occur in UNE. Fibers destined for the FCU, PUC, and DUC lie in discrete fascicles at the elbow in a deep dorsolateral position, making them less susceptible to injury in UNE and complicating differentiation from UNW. [24] Involvement of the entire ring finger or complete sparing should prompt consideration of cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- History and Physical
content: Progression of ulnar neuropathy may result in persistent numbness and paresthesia, accompanied by weakness of the muscles innervated by the ulnar nerve. Initial weakness often presents as clumsiness and reduced hand dexterity, later advancing to decreased handgrip and pinch strength, as demonstrated by a positive Froment sign. Severe cases may exhibit atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles and clawing of the fourth and fifth digits, classically described as claw hand. [25]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- History and Physical
content: Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist and hand may manifest as purely sensory, purely motor, or mixed deficits. The most common presentation involves compression of the deep palmar branch. Ulnar neuropathies of the wrist and hand are classified into 3 types. Type I lesions occur just proximal to or within the Guyon canal, affecting both deep and superficial branches, producing mixed motor and sensory deficits with weakness of all ulnar hand muscles. Type II lesions involve the deep branch exclusively, causing a pure motor deficit with a variable pattern of weakness depending on the compression site. Type III lesions are limited to the superficial branch, resulting in purely sensory deficits of the palmar aspect of the medial one-half of the fourth digit and the fifth digit. Sensory loss in Type I and Type III lesions spares the dorsal hand and fingers and the hypothenar eminence due to proximal innervation from the DUC and PUC, respectively. [26]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Evaluation
content: Diagnosis of ulnar neuropathy traditionally depends on clinical history, physical examination, and electrodiagnostic studies. Combined use of electromyography and nerve conduction studies improves diagnostic accuracy by localizing sites of pathological compression, allowing relatively early identification in patients with symptoms indicative of ulnar nerve lesions.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Evaluation
content: Ultrasound has been proposed as a screening and follow-up imaging modality for patients with UNE, as it can detect morphologic changes and determine the extent of nerve lesions. A recent meta-analysis demonstrated that in healthy participants, the ulnar nerve cross-sectional area at various locations around the elbow rarely exceeds 10 mm, providing a potential cutoff for diagnosing ulnar nerve entrapment in this region. [27]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Evaluation
content: Beyond cross-sectional area, evidence indicates that nerve diameter assessed via neuromuscular ultrasound is likely accurate for diagnosing UNE. [28] Another study revealed that measuring ulnar nerve cross-sectional area with magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasound 10 mm proximal to the medial epicondyle allows discrimination between patients with and without UNE using a threshold of 11 mm. [29] The ulnar nerve swelling ratio has been proposed as a complementary diagnostic tool. Additional sonographic indicators include intraneural vascularity, increased flattening ratio, and enlarged intraneural hypoechoic fraction, though further research is required. [30] Neuromuscular ultrasound also facilitates the identification of lesions, eg, ganglion cysts, lipomas, and other compressive masses, that may affect the nerve along its course.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Evaluation
content: In diagnosing UNE, expert consensus recommends performing both electrodiagnostic testing and ultrasound in all evaluations. Electrodiagnostic assessment should include nerve conduction studies. Ultrasound should evaluate the nerve cross-sectional area, nerve mobility, and the entire course of the ulnar nerve. [31]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Treatment / Management -- Noninvasive Treatment
content: Conservative management of UNE focuses on reducing external compression of the ulnar nerve and minimizing repetitive elbow flexion, thereby decreasing mechanical stress on the nerve. Physical therapy modalities, including cold application, neurodynamic mobilization, pulsed ultrasound, strengthening exercises, patient education, and activity or ergonomic modifications, demonstrate benefit in patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms. [32] Additional noninvasive approaches, such as ultrasound therapy and low-level laser therapy, have been shown to improve treatment outcomes. [33] [34] Splinting with an elbow brace that limits flexion constitutes another conservative strategy. Pooled analyses indicate that splinting results in symptom improvement in approximately 89% of patients with UNE. [35]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Treatment / Management -- Injections
content: Injection-based interventions have also been proposed for UNE management. Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections at the elbow have produced mixed results. [36] [37] A meta-analysis reported that injections of steroid–lidocaine mixtures improved symptoms in 54% of treated patients. Perineural injection with 5% dextrose is an alternative injectate. Compared with normal saline, perineural 5% dextrose injections yielded superior improvements in pain, disability, ulnar motor conduction velocity, and ulnar nerve cross-sectional area. [38] Both steroid and perineural dextrose injections are effective, but dextrose demonstrates greater reductions in symptom severity and cross-sectional area of the ulnar nerve. [39]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Surgical intervention is indicated for patients with persistent, progressive, or severe symptoms, including muscle atrophy. Techniques described include simple decompression, anterior transposition, and medial epicondylectomy. A systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that simple decompression and decompression with transposition are equally effective in idiopathic UNE. However, decompression with transposition is associated with a higher incidence of wound infections compared with simple decompression. [40] Low- to moderate-certainty evidence indicates minimal differences in functional improvement or surgical complications between simple decompression and subcutaneous or submuscular transposition, even in cases of severe nerve impairment. [41]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Treatment / Management -- Emerging Therapies
content: A small randomized controlled trial demonstrated that postsurgical electrical stimulation increased motor unit number and enhanced intrinsic muscle strength 3 years postoperatively. [42] These findings suggest that electrical stimulation may support long-term functional recovery after ulnar nerve surgery.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis of UNE includes C8 radiculopathy, brachial plexopathy, and medial epicondylosis. Sensory abnormalities in the forearm suggest cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy rather than UNE. Medial elbow pain may occur in both UNE and medial epicondylosis. However, UNE typically presents with paresthesias, whereas predominant pain often indicates a focal musculoskeletal injury. Sparing of the DUC and PUC may result in paresthesias localized primarily to the fingers rather than the ventral or dorsal aspects of the hand, aiding in differentiation of UNE from UNW. [43]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Staging
content: The McGowan classification, as modified by Goldberg, may be used to differentiate mild, moderate, and severe CTS. This system demonstrates moderate intra-observer and interobserver reliability and shows moderate correlation with objective sensory-motor function and motor conduction velocity. [44] Grade I is characterized by purely subjective symptoms, eg, paresthesia, without motor deficits. Grade II involves muscle weakness or objective sensory findings, subdivided into IIA, with no intrinsic muscle atrophy, and IIB, with some atrophy of the intrinsic muscles. Grade III presents with pronounced sensory and motor deficits accompanied by marked atrophy of the intrinsic muscles. [45]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for mild ulnar neuropathy is generally favorable, with early intervention critical to prevent progression. Conservative treatment is indicated for patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms. In patients with mild symptoms, nonoperative management has demonstrated benefit in approximately 90% of cases, whereas only 38% of patients with moderate symptoms respond adequately to conservative measures. [46]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Prognosis
content: In untreated mild and moderate cases of UNE, approximately one-half of patients reported symptom improvement, although activity modifications, eg, avoiding prolonged elbow flexion or repetitive movements, may have contributed to recovery. [47] Negative prognostic factors include high occupational force demands, smoking, obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), female sex, and distal upper-extremity fractures. [48]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Prognosis
content: A retrospective multicenter study evaluated outcomes of 4 surgical approaches for CTS: open or endoscopic in situ decompression, and subcutaneous or submuscular anterior transposition. Intramuscular transposition and medial epicondylectomy were excluded due to fibrosis and pain, respectively. Across procedures, over 90% of patients achieved cure or symptomatic improvement. Submuscular anterior transposition was associated with recurrence, while complication rates did not differ significantly between subcutaneous anterior transposition and in situ decompression. [49]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Complications
content: Patient outcomes are less favorable in chronic and severe cases. Complications of longstanding ulnar neuropathy, particularly with severe nerve injury, include intrinsic hand muscle atrophy, weakness, claw deformity, numbness, chronic pain or paresthesia, and loss of hand and finger dexterity, which may result in functional impairment and disability. Postoperative complications following UNE surgery include iatrogenic injury to the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, nerve subluxation, and symptom recurrence. [50]

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education should emphasize activity modification to reduce repetitive elbow flexion, ergonomic adjustments to minimize nerve compression, and sleeping position changes or splinting to prevent prolonged stretching or pressure on the nerve during full elbow flexion. Counseling should also address modifiable risk factors, including smoking cessation and weight management.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Ulnar neuropathy describes functional impairment of the ulnar nerve along its course from the brachial plexus to the hand, most commonly at the cubital tunnel but also at the wrist, forearm, and upper arm. Compression, traction, or repetitive mechanical stress may lead to sensory disturbances, motor weakness, and, in advanced cases, intrinsic hand muscle atrophy and deformity. Early recognition, prevention of prolonged compression, and timely intervention are essential, as outcomes decline once axonal injury develops. Diagnostic accuracy improves when clinicians integrate clinical examination with electrodiagnostic testing and neuromuscular ultrasound to identify the precise site and severity of nerve involvement.

title: Ulnar Neuropathy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: High-quality, patient-centered care requires coordinated efforts across the interprofessional team. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners must select appropriate diagnostic strategies, determine the need for conservative management or referral for surgical evaluation, and guide individualized treatment plans. Nurses reinforce education, monitor symptom progression, and support adherence to splinting, activity modification, and rehabilitation. Physical and occupational therapists provide targeted exercises, ergonomic interventions, and functional retraining. Pharmacists assist with medication safety and optimization, particularly when managing pain or neuropathic symptoms. Effective communication and shared decision-making across all disciplines promote early detection, reduce complications, improve functional outcomes, and strengthen team performance in managing ulnar neuropathy.
